results.authors: Chabriat H, Joutel A, Dichgans M, Tournier-Lasserve E, Bousser MG.
results.key_finding: CADASIL is caused by cysteine-altering NOTCH3 mutations (chromosome 19p13) and is the most common monogenic cause of ischaemic stroke and vascular dementia in adults. Ischaemic episodes, mostly subcortical lacunar infarcts, usually begin between 40 and 60 years; migraine with aura is the first symptom in 20 to 40 percent of patients. White matter hyperintensities are present in almost all symptomatic patients.

output.summary: CADASIL (NOTCH3, chromosome 19p13) is the most common hereditary cerebral small vessel disease. Typical features are subcortical lacunar infarcts from mid-adulthood, migraine with aura as an early symptom in a minority, cognitive decline, and white matter hyperintensities that become confluent and characteristically involve the anterior temporal lobes and the external capsules. Diagnosis is confirmed by NOTCH3 sequencing. No disease-modifying treatment exists; vascular risk factors are managed as in other small vessel disease.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No haemorrhage; bilateral periventricular white matter hypodensity disproportionate for age; equivocal subtle hypodensity in the left corona radiata.
action_criteria.label: Obtain an emergent non-contrast head CT to exclude haemorrhage before the reperfusion decision
action_criteria.rationale: Intracranial haemorrhage is the one imaging finding that forbids IV thrombolysis; the CT is the first study in every stroke alert.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Glucose 94 mg/dL (no hypoglycaemic mimic), INR 1.0, platelets 274, creatinine 0.92, troponin 0.01: no laboratory barrier to thrombolysis; LDL 122 mg/dL.
action_criteria.label: Check glucose before thrombolysis and send CBC, coagulation, creatinine and baseline troponin
action_criteria.rationale: Only the glucose must be known before thrombolysis; the other results are not awaited in a patient with no anticoagulant or suspected coagulopathy.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal sinus rhythm at 74 bpm with normal intervals; no atrial fibrillation and no ischaemic change.
action_criteria.label: Obtain a 12-lead ECG
action_criteria.rationale: Atrial fibrillation or acute myocardial ischaemia would change the mechanism and the secondary prevention; the ECG does not delay reperfusion.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No large vessel occlusion, no intracranial stenosis, no cervical stenosis or dissection: no thrombectomy target and no large artery mechanism.
action_criteria.label: Obtain CT angiography of the head and neck without waiting for creatinine
action_criteria.rationale: Vessel imaging decides thrombectomy and excludes a large artery or dissection mechanism in a 47-year-old; it does not delay IV thrombolysis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Acute left corona radiata lacunar infarct extending to the posterior limb of the internal capsule; confluent white matter hyperintensities with anterior temporal pole and external capsule involvement; chronic lacunes in both thalami, pons and right basal ganglia.
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with DWI and FLAIR after the reperfusion decision to characterise the small vessel disease
action_criteria.rationale: The white matter topography (anterior temporal poles, external capsules) and the burden of old lacunes are what separate a hereditary small vessel disease from sporadic disease here; the MRI must not delay thrombolysis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal LV size and function (LVEF 55 percent), normal left atrium, no thrombus, no significant valve disease, intact septum on the resting study: no cardioembolic source.
action_criteria.label: Obtain a transthoracic echocardiogram
action_criteria.rationale: Excluding a cardiac source completes the mechanism work-up before the infarct is attributed to small vessel disease.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sinus rhythm throughout 24 hours; no atrial fibrillation or flutter.
action_criteria.label: Monitor the cardiac rhythm for at least 24 hours on the stroke unit
action_criteria.rationale: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation would change the mechanism and the antithrombotic choice; a lacunar infarct with a determined small vessel cause does not need prolonged monitoring.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Antiphospholipid antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, homocysteine, ANA, ANCA, ESR and CRP all normal: no acquired prothrombotic or inflammatory cause.
action_criteria.label: Screen for acquired causes of stroke in a young adult: antiphospholipid antibodies, homocysteine and a vasculitis screen
action_criteria.rationale: At 47 an antiphospholipid syndrome, hyperhomocysteinaemia or a vasculitis can also cause small vessel infarcts; inherited venous thrombophilias (factor V Leiden, protein C and S) are not indicated for an arterial lacunar infarct.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Heterozygous pathogenic NOTCH3 variant c.397C>T p.(Arg133Cys), a cysteine-altering variant in EGF-like repeat 3: confirms CADASIL.
action_criteria.label: Order NOTCH3 genetic testing after pre-test counselling
action_criteria.rationale: A lacunar stroke at 47 with white matter disease disproportionate for age, anterior temporal pole involvement and an autosomal dominant history of early stroke and dementia (mother, brother) meets the indication for NOTCH3 testing.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sumatriptan is contraindicated after stroke or TIA and must be stopped; no clinically significant interaction between aspirin, atorvastatin and his medication list.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give IV thrombolysis before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial haemorrhage.
Do not give IV thrombolysis if INR is above 1.7, the platelet count is below 100,000 or another guideline contraindication is present.
Do not withhold or delay IV thrombolysis to obtain MRI or genetic results; suspected CADASIL is not a contraindication.
Do not start anticoagulation (warfarin, a DOAC or heparin) for secondary prevention without atrial fibrillation; it is not indicated in CADASIL and adds bleeding risk.
Do not resume sumatriptan or start another triptan or an ergot derivative after this stroke.
required_recommendations: Establish last known well (about 2 hours before arrival) and the NIHSS (4).

IV thrombolysis: give (about 2 hours from last known well, no haemorrhage on CT, glucose 94 mg/dL, INR 1.0, platelets 274), because weakness of the dominant right hand and arm with dysarthria is disabling for him; suspected CADASIL is not a contraindication. Thrombectomy: not indicated because CTA shows no large vessel occlusion.

Give alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (maximum 90 mg) or tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (maximum 25 mg) with a door-to-needle time under 60 minutes; blood pressure 148/86 mmHg needs no lowering before treatment, then keep it below 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours.
Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours.

Start single antiplatelet therapy (aspirin 75 to 100 mg daily, or clopidogrel 75 mg daily) 24 hours after thrombolysis once follow-up imaging excludes haemorrhage; no dual antiplatelet therapy (NIHSS 4) and no anticoagulation without atrial fibrillation.
Start a high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40 to 80 mg daily) for LDL 122 mg/dL, and treat blood pressure to a long-term target below 130/80 mmHg after the acute phase.
Stop sumatriptan permanently (contraindicated after ischaemic stroke); treat migraine attacks with non-vasoconstrictive analgesia and avoid triptans and ergot derivatives.
Refer for genetic counselling once the NOTCH3 variant is confirmed, and offer counselling and predictive testing to at-risk adult first-degree relatives.

key_clinical_evidence: Last known well about 2 hours before arrival and a disabling deficit (NIHSS 4, cannot write with the dominant hand): IV thrombolysis after the CT excludes haemorrhage; CTA shows no large vessel occlusion, so no thrombectomy.

Bilateral symmetric FLAIR white matter hyperintensities with prominent anterior temporal lobe and external capsule involvement in a patient under 55 years are not characteristic of hypertensive microangiopathy — this topographic pattern is a hallmark of CADASIL and should prompt genetic evaluation

Autosomal dominant family history of early stroke and dementia (mother and brother) in a first-degree pedigree is a major diagnostic clue for CADASIL; this distinguishes it from sporadic small vessel disease

Migraine with aura is the typical early symptom of CADASIL (20 to 40 percent of patients). This patient has migraine without aura, which is common in the general population and unspecific, so his migraine does not point to CADASIL; the diagnosis rests on the MRI pattern and the family history.
CTA, ECG, echocardiography and cardiac monitoring exclude large artery and cardioembolic mechanisms (TOAST) before the infarct is attributed to a hereditary small vessel disease.
CADASIL does not itself contraindicate IV thrombolysis; the same acute stroke protocol applies while the genetic mechanism is being investigated

Secondary prevention in CADASIL is antiplatelet-based (aspirin or clopidogrel); anticoagulation should not be started without confirmed atrial fibrillation — distinction from cardioembolic stroke prevention is clinically important
Thrombolysis is not delayed for MRI or genetic testing: the NOTCH3 result explains the mechanism and guides counselling of the family, not the acute decision.

AHA/ASA 2026 sequencing: glucose is checked before thrombolysis, but routine CBC/coagulation results are not awaited without a reason to expect abnormality; ECG/troponin do not delay reperfusion, and CTA/CTP do not wait for creatinine.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: middle-aged man with acute lacunar infarct in whom the standard embolic workup is entirely negative; the key diagnostic challenge is recognising the characteristic MRI white matter topography (anterior temporal lobe + external capsule FLAIR WMH) plus autosomal dominant family history as pointing to CADASIL, then ordering NOTCH3 genetic panel to confirm. Three grounded red herrings (migraine, mild dyslipidaemia, admission BP) create plausible alternative anchors.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Andreas Weiss is a 47-year-old right-handed White European man who presents to the emergency department via ambulance with acute-onset right arm weakness and slurred speech beginning approximately 2 hours before arrival. He was at home grading papers when he noticed his right hand was clumsy and he could not hold his pen properly. Over 10-15 minutes the weakness spread to involve his right arm, and his wife noticed his speech became slurred. He denies loss of consciousness, seizure, headache at onset, or neck pain. He reports a history of migraine without aura since age 28, occurring 2-3 times per month and well-controlled with sumatriptan. He has been an otherwise healthy, active man with no prior cardiovascular diagnoses. His wife is visibly distressed: she discloses that his mother was diagnosed with dementia in her early 50s and has had multiple strokes, and his 52-year-old brother has recently been diagnosed with recurrent small strokes and is developing cognitive decline. She asks directly whether there is a hereditary condition that could explain both the brother's illness and her husband's current presentation. The patient has not undergone brain imaging previously. He is a former smoker (quit at age 40 after a 10 pack-year history) and drinks approximately 10 units of alcohol per week socially. He takes no regular medications other than sumatriptan on demand. There is no recent trauma, no chiropractic neck manipulation, and no illicit drug use. Last known well time is established at approximately 2 hours before ED arrival.
